handoff.purpose: Complete the write-gate: unresolved-import check, baseline order, run_checks fail-closed loop, and with_markers convenience.

symbols.name: unresolved_first_party_imports
symbols.note: Static AST scan for first-party imports that name no module or name. Returns deduplicated list of messages.

symbols.name: imports_resolve
symbols.note: Gate wrapper: calls unresolved_first_party_imports and formats a refusal capped at policy.max_named_imports.

symbols.name: BASELINE
symbols.note: Tuple of the five baseline guards in a deliberately ordered sequence.

symbols.name: run_checks
symbols.note: Runs baseline plus extras; catches any exception from a check and returns a refusal. Returns '' when all pass.

symbols.name: with_markers
symbols.note: Returns a copy of the policy with elision_markers replaced by the given markers.

claims.text: First-party imports in ``content`` that name nothing in the tree.
claims.why: The function scans ast.Import and ast.ImportFrom nodes, resolves modules via _module_path, and reports both missing modules and missing names, so it does return imports that name nothing in the tree.

claims.text: MEASURED 2026-07-30. Twenty agents wrote test modules against source files they were given, and three of seven imported things that do not exist: ``daedalus.linting`` (it is ``daedalus.gui.lint``), ``ShiftManager`` from ``daedalus.shift`` (the class is ``Shift``), and ``daedalus.wiki_vault`` (it is ``daedalus.wiki.vault``).
claims.why: The measurement is historical context; this chunk cannot verify the agent study. The examples are consistent with the code's behavior, but the claim itself is not testable here.

claims.text: All three are valid Python, so a syntax gate passes them, and all three reported ``status: done``.
claims.why: The syntax gate is not in this chunk, and the status reporting is elsewhere; the claim is about other components.

claims.text: The check is STATIC on purpose. Importing the file to find out whether its imports resolve would execute module-level code from an untrusted lane -- the one thing this repository refuses to do to decide whether to trust something.
claims.why: The function only calls ast.parse and walks the AST; it never imports the target module. It uses _module_path and _exports, which are static filesystem/parse operations, not imports.

claims.text: Conservative by construction, because a false refusal costs real work: only first-party roots are judged; a missing MODULE is reported, since that cannot be a re-export; a missing NAME is reported only when the module has no star-import and no module-level ``__getattr__``.
claims.why: The code filters by roots (lines 302, 307), reports missing modules (lines 303, 309), and skips names when _exports returns opaque (line 316, which corresponds to star-import or __getattr__).

claims.text: a parse failure is a different guard's business
claims.why: The function catches (SyntaxError, ValueError, RecursionError) and returns [] without reporting, leaving parse failures to the parses guard in BASELINE.

claims.text: relative imports resolve against a package
claims.why: The code skips ImportFrom nodes with node.level (relative imports) or without node.module, so relative imports are not judged.

claims.text: `from daedalus import shift` binds a SUBMODULE, which is perfectly valid and is named nowhere in the package's __init__.py. Measured: without this the check fired on 40 of 223 real files in this repo -- a false-positive rate that would have made the gate useless and, worse, trained everyone to ignore it.
claims.why: The code explicitly checks _module_path(root, f"{node.module}.{alias.name}") and skips the name if that submodule exists, so a submodule import is not reported as missing.

claims.text: Deduplicated but order-preserving: the same bad import repeated ten times is one problem, and the first occurrence is the one worth naming.
claims.why: The function returns list(dict.fromkeys(bad)), which removes duplicates while preserving first occurrence order.

claims.text: Checked for CREATED files too -- a brand-new test module against an invented API is exactly the failure this catches, and it has no original to compare against.
claims.why: imports_resolve calls unresolved_first_party_imports on attempt.proposed directly, with no comparison to any original; it applies to any WriteAttempt, including created files.

claims.text: Cheapest first. Order is load-bearing in one direction only -- the refusal a caller sees should be the most specific one available, and "does not parse" is more useful than "82% of definitions vanished" when both are true.
claims.why: BASELINE is ordered as not_truncated, no_elision, parses, not_substituted, imports_resolve. run_checks returns on the first non-empty reason, so the earliest, most specific guard wins.

claims.text: Run the baseline, then any lane-specific additions. "" means write it.
claims.why: The loop iterates over (*BASELINE, *extra) and returns '' only if no check returns a non-empty reason.

claims.text: FAIL-CLOSED, and this is the part worth not losing: a check that raises is reported as a refusal naming the crash. The alternative -- letting the exception propagate, or catching it and continuing -- turns a broken guard into a silent permission, which is how a gate ends up passing a file that destroyed a module.
claims.why: The try/except catches Exception, returns a message naming the check and the exception, and returns that as a refusal. It does not propagate and does not continue to later checks.

claims.text: A lane may pass ``extra`` to ADD checks. There is deliberately no argument for removing one from the baseline.
claims.why: The signature has only extra: Iterable[Check] = (); there is no parameter to remove baseline checks, and the loop always includes BASELINE.

claims.text: ``policy`` with this lane's own elision markers. Convenience only.
claims.why: with_markers returns replace(policy, elision_markers=tuple(markers)), which is a copy with only that field changed.

claims.text: Grounding a model's PROSE against the tree -- audit_references, judge -- lives in daedalus/lanes/grounding.py. It was briefly here, and being here made this module two things: a write gate that refuses, and a report measurement that observes. Different subject, different consumer.
claims.why: The claim refers to another module and to history; this chunk cannot verify the existence of grounding.py or the prior location.

observations.what: unresolved_first_party_imports catches (SyntaxError, ValueError, RecursionError) but not MemoryError; a pathological input could raise MemoryError and escape the guard, though the fail-closed run_checks wrapper would still catch it and refuse.

The check skips relative imports entirely (node.level), so a relative import that names a nonexistent module inside the package is not reported. The docstring says 'relative imports resolve against a package', which is true, but the code never verifies that resolution; a genuinely broken relative import passes. This is a deliberate scope choice, not a bug.
imports_resolve caps the message at policy.max_named_imports and appends '(+N more)', but there is no check that max_named_imports is non-negative; a negative value would produce a nonsense message.

The docstring says 'a missing NAME is reported only when the module has no star-import and no module-level __getattr__', and the code checks _exports(path) which returns opaque for those cases. The correctness of that depends on _exports in another chunk; this chunk cannot verify that _exports actually detects __getattr__.

run_checks catches Exception, which includes KeyboardInterrupt? No, KeyboardInterrupt is BaseException, not Exception. A check that raises KeyboardInterrupt would propagate out, violating the fail-closed claim. But that is arguably correct for an interrupt.

The comment says 'Order is load-bearing in one direction only', but the order also determines which refusal message the caller sees when multiple guards fail; that is the stated direction. The comment is accurate.

risks: line 299 | low | MemoryError not caught in unresolved_first_party_imports, but run_checks would catch it; still, the function's own contract says parse failures return [] and this would raise instead | confirm that run_checks is always the caller; otherwise a direct call could crash
line 306 | low | relative imports are never checked for existence; a broken relative import passes the gate | decide whether the policy intends to check relative imports; if so, this is a gap
line 335 | low | max_named_imports could be negative, producing a malformed message | confirm policy construction always sets it non-negative

line 316 | medium | the missing-name suppression depends on _exports correctly detecting star-imports and __getattr__; if _exports misses one, a false positive fires | inspect _exports in the earlier chunk of this file

line 365 | low | run_checks does not catch BaseException, so a check raising KeyboardInterrupt or SystemExit would propagate, not fail closed | confirm the policy intends to treat interrupts as refusals; otherwise the docstring's 'a check that raises' is overbroad
